section_summary: This section gathers intelligence on Japanese military readiness in 1941–42, including air-defense organization, troop deployments, logistical weaknesses, and the expansion of forces in Indochina. It also documents Anglo-American efforts to assess Japan’s wartime economic potential, especially access to strategic minerals, food, fuel, industrial capacity, and transportation under blockade conditions. The largest group of documents consists of S. H. Dawes’s detailed strategic surveys of Hokkaido and the Russian Far East, including ports, railways, factories, garrisons, fortifications, airfields, and naval bases; several items appear in duplicate.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter on German technicians traveling to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that German technical specialists from South America were being sent to Japanese war-production plants.
subfiles.summary: Confidential letter: technically trained Germans in South America left for Japan via Siberia to work in war factories, continuing after the German-Soviet rupture.

subfiles.title: Foochow telegram on Japanese construction and coastal guns at Hai T'an
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese transport of timber to Hai T'an Island for barracks and the installation of long-range guns overlooking the Formosa Strait.
subfiles.summary: Foochow: small Japanese vessels carried planks and poles; Japanese naval units restricted junk traffic to Hai T'an Island, where barracks and coastal guns were being built.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Foochow telegram on Hai T'an defenses
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the report on Japanese barracks and coastal artillery on Hai T'an Island.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate Foochow telegram: timber moved to Hai T'an Island and long-range guns placed to command Formosa Strait waters.

subfiles.title: War Department radiogram estimating available Japanese divisions
subfiles.about: Transmits a British military attaché’s estimate of Japanese divisions, tank regiments, and strategic reserves.
subfiles.summary: War Department estimate: Japan has 49 divisions available, 54 by end of August and 69 after mobilization, with a fifteen-division reserve.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram no. 1380 on establishment of an air-defense bureau
subfiles.about: Reports approval of a Home Ministry air-defense bureau and Japanese press criticism of inadequate civil-defense planning.
subfiles.summary: The Privy Council approved an ordinance creating an air-defense bureau in the Home Ministry. Yomiuri and Nichi Nichi editorials emphasized vulnerability to incendiary bombing, urged fire-prevention training rather than excessive shelter construction, and called for public confidence and calm.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Tokyo telegram no. 1380
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to Grew’s telegram no. 1380 concerning the new Home Ministry air-defense bureau.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 1380: a September 3 ordinance created an air-defense bureau in the Home Ministry.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram no. 1452 on the National Defense Headquarters
subfiles.about: Describes the organization, authority, and senior appointments of Japan’s National Defense Headquarters.
subfiles.summary: The new commander-in-chief was to control army and air units defending Japan proper, Korea, Taiwan, and Karafuto while remaining responsible to the war minister and army chief of staff. General Otozō Yamada was commander-in-chief and Lieutenant General Torashirō Kawabe chief of staff; Kawabe publicly stressed air-defense preparation and national cooperation.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché telegram on creation of the National Defense General Headquarters
subfiles.about: Relays the Japanese War Office announcement creating a headquarters to command army units assigned to homeland defense.
subfiles.summary: Naval attaché reports General Yamada will also command the new National Defense General Headquarters for Japan proper, Korea, Taiwan and Karafuto; its relation to Imperial Headquarters is unclear.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence transmittal concerning Wilhelm Schmidt
subfiles.doc_type: letter of transmittal and records routing sheet
subfiles.from: Brigadier General Sherman Miles, Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: Transmits material on Wilhelm Schmidt based on information volunteered by Alfred T. Pepper.
subfiles.summary: Sherman Miles forwarded information for Berle’s consideration and any action he deemed advisable. The referenced enclosure concerned Wilhelm Schmidt and information supplied by Alfred T. Pepper, while the second page records subsequent State Department file-routing activity.

subfiles.title: Tokyo radiogram on prospective reinforcement of Japanese forces in Indochina
subfiles.about: Reports indications that Japan intended to increase its forces in Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo radiogram: Japanese forces in Indochina likely to increase soon; unclear whether strength will exceed the defense agreement.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting information on the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: Transmits an FBI memorandum containing outside-source information about the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards a November 15 memorandum on the Japanese Army to Naval Intelligence and G-2.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Army supplies and morale
subfiles.about: Reports alleged shortages, vulnerable shipping, and low morale in Japanese forces in Manchukuo and China.
subfiles.summary: Source claims Japanese armies on the Asiatic mainland had only four to six weeks of food and ammunition on October 1, 1941, with low morale and fear of submarines.

subfiles.title: London telegram no. 5727 requesting data on Japanese war potential
subfiles.about: Requests extensive American economic intelligence for a British study of Japan’s capacity to sustain military operations under blockade.
subfiles.summary: London's Ministry of Economic Warfare seeks data on Japan's iron, steel, coal, synthetic oil, labor, transport, stockpiles and morale, with questions on Manchukuo, Korea, China, Indochina, Thailand and Tonkin.

subfiles.title: Division of European Affairs memorandum on London telegram no. 5727
subfiles.about: Proposes assembling available government studies in response to Britain’s request for Japanese economic intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Memo says much of the information requested by London is unavailable in Far Eastern Affairs; studies from Military Intelligence, Export Control and Commerce could be compiled.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum to Mr. Atherton on Japanese economic information
subfiles.from: Theodore C. Achilles, Division of European Affairs
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy discussing how to obtain information requested by the Ministry of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate memo to Atherton: lacks much requested information; recommends drawing on Military Intelligence, Export Control, Commerce and Far Eastern studies.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum assigning economic research responsibility
subfiles.about: Recommends that a new economic division handle London’s request while noting possible assistance from the Coordinator of Information.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Division argues the research belongs in Acheson's special economic divisions, offering help; Remer's office has relevant material.

subfiles.title: Collado memorandum proposing collection of Japanese economic intelligence
subfiles.about: Proposes a coordinated review of existing reports and files to answer Britain’s questions about Japan.
subfiles.summary: Collado recommended examining the Maxwell report, consulting Shoemaker and Hunsberger, searching State Department files, and checking material held by the Coordinator of Information. He suggested that Mr. Jones lead the collection effort with help from Mr. Corbett and that Tokyo be asked to fill remaining gaps.

subfiles.title: London radiogram on Japanese combat strength and deployment
subfiles.about: Estimates the strength, composition, and geographic distribution of Japanese and allied forces.
subfiles.summary: London radiogram estimates Japanese combat strength at about 1,370,400, or 2,316,400 including army troops, puppet forces and Manchukuo troops, with deployment by area.

subfiles.title: Charge-out card for Great Britain despatch no. 2195
subfiles.about: Records the circulation of a despatch containing the Ministry of Economic Warfare’s survey of Japan’s economic and industrial position.
subfiles.summary: Charge-out card for Great Britain Despatch No. 2195 (November 27, 1941) on Japanese economic capacity and a Ministry of Economic Warfare survey.

subfiles.title: London telegram no. 272, section one, on gains from occupied territories
subfiles.about: Summarizes a secret British assessment of Japan’s economic gains from territorial occupation.
subfiles.summary: The Ministry of Economic Warfare judged that occupation brought Japan definite gains in tin and rubber and potential access to chrome, manganese, phosphates, and antimony, subject to transportation. The first section estimates supplies of rice, maize, and rubber that Japan might obtain without interruption.

subfiles.title: State Department paraphrase of London telegram no. 272
subfiles.about: Provides a fuller paraphrase of the British estimate of resources gained through Japan’s occupation of Thailand and Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Winant's London report estimates Japanese access to rubber, tungsten, tin, coal and other goods, with oil and nickel the principal deficiencies and shortages of copper, lead and iron ore.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on responsibility for replying to London
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Argues that technical economic drafting should be handled by the Board of Economic Operations rather than the political division.
subfiles.summary: The Far Eastern Division maintained that technical economic work lay outside its proper political function, particularly after creation of specialized economic divisions. It assigned primary responsibility for the reply to the Board of Economic Operations while offering policy advice and other assistance.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on responsibility for the London reply
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy assigning the technical economic reply to the Board of Economic Operations.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the argument that technical economic drafting should pass from the Far Eastern political division to specialized economic offices. The division nevertheless offers consultation where economic issues bear on Far Eastern policy.

subfiles.title: Vancouver despatch transmitting S. H. Dawes’s notes
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.about: Transmits strategic notes on Hokkaido and the Russian Far East prepared by former British Consular Agent S. H. Dawes.
subfiles.summary: Vancouver despatch: Dawes, former British Consular Agent at Otaru until 1940, supplied notes to British military authorities; the consulate offers extra copies.

subfiles.title: A Few Notes on the Maritime Provinces of Eastern Siberia
subfiles.about: Describes climate, harbors, seaplane bases, and armed motor-boat stations on the Russian Far Eastern coast.
subfiles.summary: Dawes outlines severe winter ice conditions and identifies coastal bases between Vladivostok and the Amur River. He evaluates Vladimir Bay, Olga Bay, Imperial Harbour, Constantine Bay, and De Castries Bay for shipping, seaplanes, torpedo boats, defenses, and vulnerability to mining or surprise attack.

subfiles.title: Dawes letter accompanying his strategic notes
subfiles.about: Delivers Dawes’s notes and offers further unpaid assistance if supplied with a suitable map.
subfiles.summary: Dawes says the British Embassy barred him from taking his map out of Japan; his information is largely personal observation, except seaplane and motor boat reports from ship captains.

subfiles.title: Hokkaido, Japan: strategic and industrial notes
subfiles.to: Paul R. Josselyn and the U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed survey of Hokkaido’s military, industrial, transportation, port, and communications infrastructure.
subfiles.summary: Drawing principally on fifteen years of personal observation, Dawes describes copper smelters, oil storage, fish-oil plants, coal handling, power stations, wireless facilities, airfields, roads, railways, repair shops, dry docks, steel and munitions works, garrisons, and fortifications. He identifies vulnerable railway junctions and concentrated administrative centers, describes troop movements through Otaru, and assesses the ports of Hakodate, Otaru, Muroran, Kushiro, and Rumoi. The report also discusses civilian air-raid training, salvage vessels, fisheries, and Japanese-operated oil wells in Russian Sakhalin.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Vancouver despatch transmitting Dawes’s notes
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the despatch forwarding S. H. Dawes’s intelligence on Hokkaido.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate Vancouver despatch transmitting Dawes's notes; British military authorities received the same material.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Dawes’s letter accompanying his notes
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy offering Dawes’s strategic information and further assistance.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Dawes's letter asking for a large-scale map to mark additional locations and distinguishing observation from captains' information.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Hokkaido, Japan: strategic and industrial notes
subfiles.to: Paul R. Josselyn and the U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of Dawes’s comprehensive strategic survey of Hokkaido.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Dawes’s descriptions of Hokkaido’s smelters, fuel and coal facilities, transportation network, ports, communications, airfields, garrisons, and fortifications. It highlights railway chokepoints and marshalling yards, the Muroran steel and munitions works, military activity at Asahikawa and Otaru, and the island’s civil-defense preparations. It concludes with information on salvage and fishing fleets and Japanese oil operations in Russian Sakhalin.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Notes on the Maritime Provinces of Eastern Siberia
subfiles.to: Paul R. Josselyn and the U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Begins another copy of Dawes’s survey of Russian Far Eastern climate, harbors, and naval-air facilities.
subfiles.summary: Dawes's August 1941 notes on Eastern Siberia's Maritime Provinces: winter ice, Russian seaplane and motor-boat bases, and coastal stations between Vladivostok and the Amur; copy continues beyond page 156.
